analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuels a per-ton carbon fee and returns the money through tax credits and benefit checks.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2017 with one cosponsor, the bill was sent to five House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee on coal, oil, and natural gas based on the carbon dioxide they release when burned — starting at $49 per ton in 2018 and rising 2% a year plus inflation until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of their 2005 level. It would also charge fluorinated gases and methane leaked or vented from fossil fuel supply chains. Most of the money would come back to households: a tax credit worth up to $550 per worker ($1,100 for couples), annual checks to Social Security beneficiaries, veterans, and disabled Americans, and $10 billion a year in state grants to help low-income and rural households with energy bills and to retrain fossil fuel workers. Part of the revenue would instead cut the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 29%.
analysis.who_benefits: Working taxpayers get a refundable credit of the lesser of 6.2% of earned income or $550 ($1,100 on joint returns), which does not count as income for other benefit programs. Social Security beneficiaries, certain veterans, and disabled individuals receive an annual payment of the same amount. Low-income and rural households get help with energy bills through state grants, and fossil fuel workers get priority for job training and transition assistance. Everyone gains from lower greenhouse gas emissions, and the carbon capture industry gains new refunds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working taxpayers, seniors, and low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for workers of the lesser of 6.2% of earned income or $550 per person ($1,100 for joint filers), indexed to inflation, and expressly disregards it when calculating eligibility for other federal and state benefit programs.

Sends an annual payment in the same amount to Social Security beneficiaries, certain veterans, and disabled individuals, certified through the Social Security Administration, the Railroad Retirement Board, and the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Appropriates $10 billion per year, inflation-adjusted, for state cost mitigation grants to help low-income and rural households with energy costs, with job training and worker transition assistance prioritized for fossil fuel industry workers.

Prices the carbon dioxide from coal, petroleum products, and natural gas at $49 per ton starting in 2018, rising 2% annually plus inflation until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of their 2005 level, and extends fees to fluorinated greenhouse gases and to methane vented, flared, or leaked across fossil fuel supply chains.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, petroleum, and natural gas producers pay the fee on every ton of carbon dioxide their products would emit, plus supplementary fees on supply-chain methane after 2020. Households and businesses pay higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, only partly offset by the credits. Energy-intensive manufacturers pay more for energy inputs, though border adjustments rebate fees on exports and match fees on competing imports. The corporate rate cut reduces federal revenue that carbon fees would otherwise return to households.

drawbacks.text: The fee raises prices for gasoline, heating, and electricity. The flat credit ($550 per person) is fixed regardless of how much energy a household uses, so families who drive long distances or heat large homes in cold climates could pay more in higher energy prices than they get back.

A significant share of the carbon fee revenue goes to cutting the corporate tax rate from 35% to 29% rather than to household rebates or public investment, reducing the amount available to offset the fee's effects on consumers.

The bill allows refunds for carbon dioxide captured and used in enhanced oil and gas recovery, meaning some captured carbon could be used to produce additional fossil fuels while still claiming the refund.
The fee keeps rising year after year as long as emissions exceed 20% of the 2005 level, with no ceiling, so the long-run cost of the policy is open-ended if emissions targets are not met.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design returns most of the money progressively: a dollar-maximum credit is worth far more to a low-wage worker than to a high earner, the credits don't count against other benefits, and low-income and rural households get direct grants. But the flat credit does not track actual energy costs, so some high-use households would lose out, and roughly a third of the revenue is redirected to a corporate tax cut that does nothing to offset energy prices. The emissions target (20% of 2005 levels) is ambitious, and the escalating fee with no ceiling is a real long-run cost if clean alternatives don't scale as hoped. On balance, the household provisions and emissions reduction outweigh the drawbacks for most people, though the corporate cut is a plain concession to business interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to five House committees and two subcommittees, and none of them ever held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on July 26, 2017, joined by Rep. David Cicilline as its only cosponsor.

The House referred it to five committees — Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Veterans' Affairs, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce — and then to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee and the Environment Subcommittee.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive manufacturers are better off because the bill never advanced — they never faced the carbon fee or supply-chain methane charges. Corporations also kept the 35% tax rate rather than the 29% rate the bill offered. The cost of inaction fell on people who would have received the credits, benefit checks, and transition assistance, and on anyone exposed to carbon emissions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, which avoided the fee

industries.industry: Coal mining and oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges a per-ton fee on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas at the mine, refinery, terminal, or port of entry, rising 2% a year, plus supplementary fees after 2020 for methane vented, flared, or leaked across their supply chains. The industry's interest in blocking the fee runs against the public's interest in lower emissions and cleaner air.

The bill cuts the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 29% on income over $75,000, funded by the carbon fee. Corporations gain the tax cut but would pay carbon fees on their energy use; the rate cut reduces the revenue available to offset energy costs for households.

The fee raises the cost of energy inputs for goods like steel, cement, and chemicals, but the bill rebates fees on exported goods and imposes an equalizing fee on competing imports, shielding manufacturers from losing ground to foreign competitors.

The bill pays refunds for every ton of carbon dioxide captured and securely stored or used in products — including enhanced oil and gas recovery — creating a revenue stream for capture projects. The enhanced-recovery use means some refunds support producing more oil.

A rising fee on fossil fuels makes wind, solar, and efficiency investments relatively cheaper, growing the market for clean energy suppliers. What benefits the industry here is the same price signal that reduces emissions for the public.
